# Outlook — a product backlog above the V-model {#sec-outlook}

This chapter is the design study, written 2026-08-27, behind a layer that records what a
*user* wants in the user's own words, above the engineering machinery of the preceding
chapters.

**Stage one shipped** (REQ-093): the backlog artifact, the capture verb, the take-up link at
intake and the acceptance verdict are built, and @sec-backlog is their reference. Everything
here is the reasoning that produced them — kept because the argument matters more than the
feature, and because two further stages are still outlook: the **retrospective** and the
**status server**.

## The question

DevSteward's unit of work is the requirement, and a requirement is already solution-shaped:
by the time `/intake` is finished, the idea has been interrogated into scope boundaries,
dependencies, and acceptance criteria that name runnable tests. That is the point — it is
what makes the engine able to certify anything at all.

But it leaves three gaps.

- **There is no cheap way in.** The only door into the method is a full `/intake`
  interview. A half-formed observation — *"the return button should be green and larger"*,
  *"I want a printout for this panel"* — has nowhere to live. It stays in a chat log and
  dies there.
- **There is no user-language layer.** Every artifact in the system is written in solution
  language. Nothing records the need in the words of the person who has it.
- **Nothing checks the built thing against the need that motivated it.** A REQ closes when
  its acceptance criteria are green. Those criteria were written by the same session that
  designed the solution, against a specification that session also wrote. The loop closes
  on itself. A system built this way can pass every check it set for itself while drifting
  away from what anyone actually asked for — and it will do so invisibly, because there is
  no artifact left that says what was asked for.

The third gap is the serious one. It is the failure mode that motivates the whole study:
*a set of self-sustaining rules and constraints that no longer reflect the actual user
requirements.*

One consumer project has already improvised a fix. DriveSteward keeps a `docs/BACKLOG.md`
of user needs in the operator's words, with a rule that an item naming a mechanism *"has
already made a decision nobody asked it to make"*, and a handle rather than a REQ id so
that listing an item commits to nothing. That file is the seed of everything below.

## The shape: two levels, not two systems

The tempting move is to put Scrum on top — a backlog, sprints, a board — and let the
V-model live inside it. That is the wrong frame, because it treats the two as separate
systems that must be joined.

They are not. The correct frame is older than both and comes from requirements
engineering: **there are two levels of requirement, and a transformation between them.**
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 defines the System Requirements Definition process as one that
transforms *"the stakeholder, user-oriented view of desired capabilities into a technical
view of a solution that meets the operational needs of the user"*, producing two
documents — a Stakeholder Requirements Specification (StRS) and a System Requirements
Specification (SyRS).

That transformation is exactly the missing step. In German engineering vocabulary it is
the move from *Lastenheft* to *Pflichtenheft*, which is a useful handle because the same
tradition states the two checks crisply: *Verifikation* asks whether the technical
requirements of the Pflichtenheft are met; *Validierung* asks whether the requirements
definition is fit for the stakeholders' goals.

| | Stakeholder level | System level |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact | backlog item | `REQ-NNN.md` |
| Language | the user's | the solution's |
| Owner | the person with the need | the engineering session |
| Written | when the need appears | at intake, by translation |
| Answers | *what do I want, and why* | *what must be true, and how is it proven* |
| Checked by | acceptance — a human verdict | verification — runnable tests |
| Standard | StRS (29148) | SyRS (29148) |

Two levels, one system. The backlog is not a second state machine bolted on top; it is the
level of requirement DevSteward never wrote down.

## Where the sprint analogy holds, and where it breaks

It is natural to call one REQ and its Design → Build → System-Test cycle a *sprint*. The
analogy is useful for anyone who arrives from agile practice, and it is nearly right. But
it breaks at one specific joint, and the break is instructive.

**A Scrum sprint fixes time and varies scope.** The time-box closes on schedule; whatever
is unfinished returns to the product backlog. A sprint therefore cannot fail — it is simply
over. **A REQ fixes scope and varies time.** It stays open until its criteria are met.

So "REQ = sprint" is an analogy about *containment*, not about *closure*. The REQ is the
unit of scope, and DevSteward has no concept of time at all.

This is not a deficiency to be corrected. It is a considered position, and it is one that
others working on agent-driven development have reached independently: the *agentic-scrum*
project rules that a sprint is one backlog item of any duration, not time-boxed, with no
velocity estimation, on the grounds that time-boxing and story points assume human
constraints that agents do not have. Two designs arriving separately at the same ruling is
worth something.

But the time-box is load-bearing in Scrum, and dropping it drops three things. Each needs a
conscious replacement:

| What the time-box buys | Replacement in DevSteward |
|---|---|
| A forced re-prioritization cadence | **Free, and better.** With no time-box, *every* intake is a planning event — the backlog can be reordered at any moment, not on a fortnightly rhythm. |
| A bounded blast radius for a bad plan | **Already present.** Lettered ids (`REQ-028p`) and the rule that a known defect is never scoped out silently — it is fixed here or homed in a named follow-on REQ — are the splitting mechanism. |
| A regular inspect-and-adapt point | **Genuinely missing.** This is the one real loss, and it is what a retrospective would restore. With no time-box, the natural trigger is the REQ land: a retrospective per REQ, not per sprint. |

Note that Scrum has *two* end-of-sprint ceremonies, and DevSteward already has one of them.
The **Sprint Review** — where the product owner inspects the increment — is the System-Test
phase with its `manual` checks. Only the **Retrospective** is absent.

## Two verdicts, not one

This is the heart of the design, and the place where the two levels earn their separation.

Today a REQ has exactly one verdict: its acceptance criteria are green or they are not. The
proposed model has **two independent verdicts, given at the same moment and recorded
separately**:

1. **REQ verification** — does the built system meet what the REQ specified? This is the
   existing gate, unchanged and still **blocking**. A red here is a defect against the
   spec: the REQ does not close, and it goes to rework. The engineering cycle must not be
   allowed to fail from the system-requirement level downward.

2. **Item acceptance** — does the delivered result satisfy the *need*, as the item's own
   acceptance criteria state it? This verdict belongs to the person with the need. It is
   **advisory to the REQ and blocking to the item.**

The second verdict is what makes the model worth building, because it can differ from the
first. A user can say *"the UI is exactly as specified"* — verification green — and in the
same breath *"but it is still not easy to use"* — acceptance denied. Both statements are
true, and today the system has no way to hold them at once.

When acceptance is denied and verification is green:

- the REQ **closes** on its verification result;
- the item **stays open** in the backlog, carrying an **attempt record**: this REQ tried to
  cover this need, and did not succeed, for this stated reason;
- the item is then available to be taken up by another REQ, reprioritized, left alone, or
  retired — entirely at the owner's discretion.

This mirrors Scrum exactly: an unaccepted backlog item returns to the product backlog; you
do not reopen the sprint. And it makes the denial *productive* rather than merely negative,
because the attempt record is the artifact that stops the next REQ from repeating the same
mistake. Without the recorded reason, a denied item is just an item that failed twice.

**The denial forks, and the fork is the V-model doing useful work at runtime:**

- The build did not match the spec → a *verification* failure → rework, the existing loop.
- The build matched the spec and the spec was wrong → the REQ closes as built-to-spec, the
  item returns to the backlog with the learning recorded, and a new intake follows.

**The hazard, and its guard.** An advisory gate is a loophole waiting to be used: *ship it,
mark the item unsatisfied, move on.* The guard is doctrine DevSteward already owns, applied
one level up — **a denial is never silent.** A denied item must, in the same act, either
name the follow-on REQ that will complete it, or be explicitly retired with a reason.

## Vocabulary, corrected

Three terms are routinely crossed when agile and V-model practice meet, and getting them
wrong here would bake the error into file formats that outlive the confusion.

**Definition of Done.** In the Scrum Guide this is a *single, product-wide quality
checklist applied to every backlog item* — stable across sprints, defined at team or
organisation level. It is never per-item. Per-item conditions of satisfaction are
**acceptance criteria**, which the Scrum Guide does not define at all; they are a
complementary practice.

The useful consequence: **DevSteward already has a Definition of Done in the correct
sense.** It is the engine's land gate — lint green, the declared suite green, the capture
gate satisfied, index and frontmatter in lockstep, everything in one commit. That checklist
applies to every REQ, is stable across REQs, and is already mechanized. There is nothing to
invent, only something to name.

**Acceptance** belongs to the user. In 15288/29148 practice, acceptance testing is the
customer's decision and sits on the validation side. So the word should be reserved for the
item level.

The resulting vocabulary, which the rest of this chapter uses:

| Term | Level | Owner | Blocking? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Definition of Done** | project-wide | the engine | yes — the land gate, every REQ |
| **Verification criteria** | REQ (`check: regression`, `check: live`) | the engineering session | yes |
| **Acceptance criteria** | backlog item | the person with the need | to the item, not the REQ |

## What DevSteward already has

The practical finding of this study is that the layer is much smaller than it first looks.
Of thirteen concepts a Scrum-shaped delivery layer would bring, DevSteward already has six,
would build three, deliberately rejects one, and three are vocabulary only.

| Scrum concept | Requirements-engineering equivalent | In DevSteward today | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product Backlog | Stakeholder requirements (StRS) | — | **build** |
| Product Backlog Item | one stakeholder requirement | — | **build** |
| Acceptance criteria (per item) | validation criteria | — | **build** |
| Product Owner | acquirer / stakeholder | the operator, informally | doctrine only |
| Sprint | *(no equivalent)* | one REQ cycle | vocabulary only |
| Sprint Backlog | System requirements (SyRS) | the REQ and its plan | have |
| Sprint Goal | — | the REQ's Requirement section | have |
| **Definition of Done** | quality gate | **the engine's land gate** | have — name it |
| Sprint Review | acceptance | System-Test, `check: manual` | have — add the item link |
| Sprint Retrospective | process improvement | — | build, separately |
| Increment | verified build | the landed commit | have |
| Story points / velocity | — | — | **reject** |
| — | verification | `check: regression`, `check: live` | have |
| — | bidirectional traceability | — | **build** |

## What was built, and what is still outlook

**Stage one — the backlog and its link to intake — shipped as REQ-093.** The reference is
@sec-backlog; what follows is why each piece has the shape it has.

- **The artifact.** A per-project backlog of items, each a need in the user's words with a
  stable handle rather than a REQ id, so that listing an item commits to nothing. Config
  seam like every other doc path, and inert when absent — a project with no user-need queue
  is not required to keep an empty file.
- **A frictionless way in.** Capture must cost nothing, or it will not happen. A one-line
  command, usable by a person or by a session recording what the operator just said, is the
  whole feature. The idea comes from a non-programmer running Claude Code who wired an
  "add to backlog" button directly into his own application, and fed it one-sentence needs.
- **The intake link.** `/intake` takes up one or more items and performs the translation
  explicitly: first author the item's acceptance criteria in user language, *then* translate
  into a requirement and its verification criteria. **The order is the point.** Criteria
  written after the solution is known get quietly bent to fit what was going to be built
  anyway — which is the failure this whole layer exists to prevent, reappearing one level
  up. Capture stays frictionless; the discipline lands at intake.
- **The acceptance verdict.** A standalone act, available at any time after the REQ lands:
  the owner records, per item, whether the delivered result satisfies its acceptance
  criteria — with a stated reason on a denial. Deliberately *not* a step inside the
  System-Test session: acceptance belongs to the person with the need rather than to the
  tester, the honest verdict on something like *"easy to use"* often arrives only after
  living with the result, and Scrum likewise keeps the Review separate from the testing.
  It also means a REQ that takes up an item does not thereby acquire a mandatory extra
  validation session.

**Stage two — the retrospective (outlook).** What went wrong, what to improve, triggered at REQ land
rather than on a cadence, feeding a project's own accumulated doctrine. Every project run
under DevSteward develops local specialties; today they live in the operator's head and in
the REQ prose. This is the least-defined part of the study and is deliberately left for a
separate design.

**Stage three — a status surface (outlook).** A small server rendering an overview across projects:
each project's state, its open backlog items, and a way to record an acceptance verdict
directly. This is a separate objective and a separate design, but it exerts one constraint
on stage one that is worth naming now: if a verdict is something a web page can record,
then recording it must be an ordinary, callable act — not a decision buried inside a
transcript. That is the practical reason acceptance is a standalone command rather than a
step inside the System-Test session.

**A field worth carrying on the item: provenance.** DriveSteward's backlog notes already
distinguish items given in the operator's words from items *"proposed by the session and
chosen by the operator from alternatives"*. That distinction is the real guard against a
system writing its own requirements and then satisfying them. It deserves to be a field
rather than a footnote.

## What would deliberately not be built

Subtraction is the harder half of the design, and most of the Scrum apparatus does not
survive contact with this method:

- **No sprint object.** No sprint file, goal, capacity, or committed-items list. The REQ is
  the container; a second one would be a second status surface above the requirements index
  — precisely the kind of artifact DevSteward has removed once already, for the reason that
  a status copy with no writer drifts.
- **No time-boxing.** Scope is fixed, time is not.
- **No story points, no velocity.** They estimate human throughput. The useful quantities
  for agent-driven work are different in kind — risk, uncertainty, validation cost, whether
  a human decision is required.
- **No agent role-play.** Some frameworks in this space instantiate a Scrum Master, a
  Product Owner and a Developer as separate agents that argue from assigned incentives. The
  product owner in this method is a person, and the value of that is precisely that they
  are not simulated.
- **No worktrees or per-task branches.** Several projects in the field isolate agent work in
  git worktrees. DevSteward removed exactly that machinery, deliberately, after it produced
  a string of failures that each added structure to patch the previous one.

## The state of the field

The Claude Code ecosystem does contain projects that put an agile layer around an
engineering pipeline. As of August 2026 they are, with GitHub stars as a rough proxy for
external adoption:

| Project | Model | Stars |
|---|---|---|
| `seanyao/roll` | backlog → tasks → agents → PR, evidence per task | 14 |
| `atusy/agentic-scrum` | AI-adapted Scrum; sprint = 1 item, not time-boxed | 8 |
| `rbah31/claude-code-workflow` | sprint-based workflow, isolated phase sessions | 5 |
| `cristian-robert/claude-code-harness` | PIV+E pipeline with an optional agile layer | 1 |
| `mohammad-shaddad/cardo` | multi-agent sprint orchestration, gated delivery | 0 |

These are single-author experiments with essentially no external adoption. That is not a
criticism — several are substantial and self-applied at real scale, and `roll` reports
3,478 commits and 435 delivered stories against itself — but it does mean the field has no
established practice yet, and none of these should be treated as an authority. They are
peers.

Four of their ideas are worth taking:

- **Gate modes — autonomous, advisory, shadow** (`cardo`). A gate that surfaces a finding
  without blocking is a distinct and useful thing, and it is exactly the shape an item
  acceptance verdict needs. Every gate DevSteward has today is blocking.
- **Sprint = one item, not time-boxed** (`agentic-scrum`). Independent confirmation of the
  ruling above.
- **A lessons file updated after every correction** (`claude-code-workflow`). A
  per-correction trigger, finer-grained than per-REQ, relevant to the retrospective.
- **Acceptance evidence per unit of work** (`roll`). DevSteward has this already as the
  evidence directory; the convergence is a good sign.

The genuinely useful references are older and lie outside the ecosystem: **ISO/IEC/IEEE
29148:2018** for the StRS→SyRS transformation and its quality attributes for stakeholder
requirements — *necessary, implementation-free, unambiguous, singular, verifiable,
traceable*, of which "implementation-free" is the rule DriveSteward's backlog derived
independently; **EARS** (Mavin et al., Rolls-Royce, RE'09) for a teachable grammar for the
translated requirement — `WHILE <precondition>, WHEN <trigger>, the <system> SHALL
<response>`; **Specification by Example / ATDD** (Adzic, Larman) as the road not taken,
where one artifact is both the user's criterion and the automated test; **dual-track agile**
(Cagan, Patton) for the discovery track that fills a backlog, which maps onto DevSteward's
concept phase; and **bidirectional traceability** as practised under ISO 26262 and DO-178C,
which is the standard name for what links a need to a requirement to a test to its evidence.

## Open questions

- **How many items may one REQ take up?** Several, in the model as stated. But an item
  denied while its siblings are accepted needs the attempt record to be per-item, not
  per-REQ.
- **Who plays product owner in a project of one?** The authority that makes a Scrum backlog
  trustworthy comes from the role being separate from the team. When operator and engineer
  are the same person, only the artifact enforces the separation — which raises the stakes
  on provenance, and on the rule that item acceptance criteria are written before the
  translation.
